From the Time Domain to the Frequency Domain

For the past few lessons, we have worked a lot with the Fourier transform. Usually, the realistic situation is that you have some kind of complicated waveform. In the actual experiments we did in class, you might have some signal x(t)—it might be the displacement of an AFM cantilever, or the tiny mechanical vibrations of a wine glass. We call this our time-domain signal.

When we feed this complicated waveform into the Fourier transform, it spits out the frequency spectrum, X(f). Notice the notation: we use a lowercase letter for our time-domain signal, which is a function of time t, and an uppercase letter for our frequency-domain spectrum, which is a function of frequency f. The Fourier transform tells you exactly what frequencies live inside your complicated waveform. It is an incredibly powerful tool. If you ever want to find out what frequencies are hiding in your data, your first go-to is the Fourier transform.

But how does this actually work? Did this ever look like magic to you when you ran the code in your homework? There is no magic in this universe—or at least, not in this class. If you break it down enough, it can all be explained by simple math.

Before we dive into the equations, remember a few lessons ago when I asked you how to find the resonance frequency of a wine glass? The first method you all thought of was to use a speaker. You set the speaker to output a specific frequency, and you look at the glass. Is it vibrating? No? You turn the knob to the next frequency. Still no vibration. You keep sweeping the frequency until, at some point, you hit the jackpot and the glass vibrates wildly.

You could do this manually, one frequency at a time, but it would take a long time. It turns out, if you look under the hood, the Fourier transform is doing exactly this! Instead of you having to test frequencies one by one, the math handles the sweep for you. Let us see how.

The Fourier Transform Algorithm by Hand

We are going to do a very silly thing first and calculate a Fourier transform by hand. We will start with a waveform that is really simple: a pure, undamped sinusoid. Let’s say we have an amplitude A_1 = 6.7 nm and a frequency f_1 = 200 Hz.

We can easily convert that frequency to a period T_1: \begin{equation} \tag{1} T_1 = \frac{1}{f_1} = \frac{1}{200 \text{ Hz}} = 0.005 \text{ s} = 5 \text{ ms} \end{equation} So, our signal completes exactly one cycle every 5 ms. We can write our time-domain signal as: \begin{equation} \tag{2} x(t) = A_1 \sin(2\pi f_1 t) = 6.7 \text{ nm} \cdot \sin(2\pi \cdot 200 \text{ Hz} \cdot t) \end{equation}

Now, I want to give you the big, scary-looking algorithm for the Fourier transform. To find the frequency spectrum X(f), we evaluate this integral: \begin{equation} \tag{3} X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) \sin(2\pi f t) \, dt \end{equation} Here, x(t) is our original signal, and \sin(2\pi f t) is what we call our reference signal (or test wave) at a specific test frequency f. We are integrating over all time t, from negative infinity to positive infinity.

You might look at this and think, "What is this abomination?" But think of this integral as a little mathematical worker inside your computer. The worker takes your signal, multiplies it by a reference signal at a specific frequency f, and then finds the total area under the resulting curve. Your computer program tries an infinite number of reference signals automatically. Today, we are just going to try a few specific reference frequencies to see what happens.

Testing a Reference Frequency: 100 Hz

Let’s ask our mathematical worker to test a reference frequency of f = 100 Hz. The corresponding period for this reference is 10 ms. As instructed by Equation 3, we need to multiply our signal x(t) by our reference signal \sin(2\pi \cdot 100 \text{ Hz} \cdot t).

Think about how this multiplication works step-by-step. When we look at a portion of time where both the signal and the reference have a positive hump, multiplying a positive value by a positive value gives us a positive product. We get a positive hump in our product curve.

What happens when the signal dips into negative territory, but the reference is still positive? A negative times a positive gives a negative. The product curve dips down into a negative hump. As we continue along the time axis, we get combinations of positive times negative (which is negative) and negative times negative (which gives a positive hump).

Because we are multiplying two oscillating functions, the resulting product curve oscillates as well. To find the value of the Fourier transform at 100 Hz, X(100 \text{ Hz}), we need to take the integral of this product curve. In calculus, the integral is simply the area under the curve.

If we look at the area under our product curve over a long time, we see that we have equal amounts of positive humps and negative humps. When we add them all up, they average out to zero! \begin{equation} \tag{4} X(100 \text{ Hz}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) \sin(2\pi \cdot 100 \text{ Hz} \cdot t) \, dt = 0 \end{equation}

In mathematics, when we multiply two functions together, integrate the product, and get zero, we say those two functions are orthogonal. You might have heard "orthogonal" used as a synonym for "perpendicular" in geometry. Two perpendicular lines have independent directions; they have nothing in common. Similarly, two orthogonal functions have very little in common. Because our 200 Hz signal and our 100 Hz reference are orthogonal, their product cancels out to zero. The mathematical worker reports back: "No 100 Hz found here."

If we tested a 50 Hz reference against our 200 Hz signal, would the mathematical worker find anything?

No, the worker would still report zero. A 50 Hz reference is also orthogonal to a 200 Hz signal. The product of the two waves creates equal positive and negative areas that cancel out when integrated over time.

To visualize this orthogonality, let’s look at a schematic of multiplying a fast sine wave by a slow sine wave.

Hitting the Jackpot: 200 Hz

Now let’s step up our reference frequency to f = 200 Hz. This is the exact frequency of our original signal. We have hit the jackpot!

When we multiply our 200 Hz signal by a 200 Hz reference, something special happens. Everywhere we look, the signs match. When the signal is positive, the reference is positive. When the signal is negative, the reference is also negative. And as we know, a negative times a negative gives a positive.

This means that the product curve consists entirely of positive humps. There is no cancellation. If we grab a crayon and shade in the area under this product curve, we just keep adding more and more positive area. \begin{equation} \tag{5} X(200 \text{ Hz}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) \sin(2\pi \cdot 200 \text{ Hz} \cdot t) \, dt = \infty \end{equation} Because we are integrating from negative infinity to positive infinity, we have an infinite amount of area. The Fourier transform at our jackpot frequency theoretically blows up to infinity.

If we try f = 300 Hz, we are back to a mismatch. The 200 Hz signal and the 300 Hz reference are orthogonal. The positive and negative humps cancel out, and the integral is zero.

Building the Spectrum

We have just calculated three points for our frequency spectrum X(f). At 100 Hz, we got zero. At 200 Hz, we got a massive spike (theoretically infinite). At 300 Hz, we got zero again. Let’s plot this out.

Now, we need to address a practical reality. When you take real data and run a Fourier transform, you get a distinct peak, but it never actually goes to infinity. Why is that?

Think about how long you actually record data. Nobody takes measurements for an infinite amount of time. We measure for a finite duration, let’s call it T. Maybe we record our voice for 2 seconds, or measure a cantilever for 67 seconds. Because our measurement time is finite, our integral gets clipped. We are actually calculating: \begin{equation} \tag{6} X(f) = \int_{0}^{T} x(t) \sin(2\pi f t) \, dt \end{equation} Since we only accumulate area for a finite time T, the peak height is finite. The longer you measure, the taller and narrower your peak becomes. If you only measure for a very short time, you get a short, wide peak.

Another factor that keeps peaks finite is damping. If your oscillator is damped, the signal decays over time. Even if you measured forever, the signal eventually dies out to zero, meaning you only have a finite amount of area to sum up. Damping smears out the peak, making it wider and shorter. But even without damping, the finite recording time guarantees our peaks never reach infinity.

If you record the vibrations of a guitar string for 2 seconds versus 10 seconds, how will the X(f) peaks differ?

The 10-second recording will produce taller, narrower peaks than the 2-second recording. Because the integral accumulates area over a longer time period T, the resulting peak grows larger. However, since neither measurement lasts forever, neither peak will reach infinity.

A More Complex Signal: Two Frequencies at Once

That was the simple baby stuff. What if we have a more complicated signal with multiple frequency components? Let’s define a new signal that contains both a 200 Hz component and a 300 Hz component, with different amplitudes: \begin{equation} \tag{7} x(t) = 6 \text{ nm} \cdot \sin(2\pi \cdot 200 \text{ Hz} \cdot t) + 3 \text{ nm} \cdot \sin(2\pi \cdot 300 \text{ Hz} \cdot t) \end{equation} If you were to plot this waveform, it looks rather messy—big humps, small humps, repeating in a complex pattern. If you were just handed this raw data, it would not be obvious what frequencies are inside it.

But we can run it through our mathematical worker again. When we test a 100 Hz reference, the product has equal positive and negative areas. The integral is zero.

When we test a 200 Hz reference, something interesting happens. The 200 Hz reference is orthogonal to the 300 Hz part of the signal, so that part cancels out to zero. But the 200 Hz reference matches the 200 Hz part of the signal! This creates a net positive area. The mathematical worker says, "Yes, I found some 200 Hz in here."

When we test a 300 Hz reference, the opposite occurs. The reference ignores the 200 Hz component (they are orthogonal) but matches the 300 Hz component, again yielding a net positive area.

Notice the difference in the amount of area generated. The 200 Hz component in our original signal has an amplitude of 6 nm, while the 300 Hz component has an amplitude of 3 nm. Because the 200 Hz component is twice as large, multiplying it by the matching reference generates twice as much area compared to the 300 Hz match.

If we plot the spectrum for this complex signal, we get two distinct spikes.

The ratio of the peak heights in the frequency domain is exactly 2:1, which matches the ratio of the amplitudes in the time domain. The Fourier transform not only tells you which frequencies are present, but also how much of each frequency is there.

Suppose we add a third component to our signal: 12 \text{ nm} \cdot \sin(2\pi \cdot 400 \text{ Hz} \cdot t). How would the peak at 400 Hz compare to the peak at 200 Hz?

The peak at 400 Hz would be exactly twice as tall as the peak at 200 Hz. The Fourier transform preserves the amplitude ratios from the time domain. Since 12 nm is double the 6 nm amplitude of the 200 Hz component, its resulting integrated area is twice as large.

The Full Picture: The Complex Exponential

Up until now, we have been using a simple sine wave as our reference signal. This is a great way to build intuition, but the actual algorithm used in professional software is slightly more sophisticated. Instead of just a sine wave, the standard Fourier transform uses a complex exponential as the test wave: \begin{equation} \tag{8} X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-i 2\pi f t} \, dt \end{equation} Thanks to Euler’s formula, we know that this complex exponential is just a combination of a cosine wave and a sine wave: \begin{equation} \tag{9} e^{-i 2\pi f t} = \cos(2\pi f t) - i\sin(2\pi f t) \end{equation} By using both cosine and sine, the algorithm can detect a frequency regardless of its phase (whether the wave starts at zero, or starts at its peak). But the core concept remains exactly the same: we multiply our signal by a test wave of frequency f, and then we average the product (find the area).

The computer simply sweeps through a huge list of test frequencies. For every single frequency f, it picks the test wave, multiplies it by your data, integrates over time, and plots that single point on the spectrum. Then it steps to the next frequency and does it all again.

This is the engine under the hood of the Fourier transform. It is not magic. It is just a very fast, very diligent mathematical worker checking every possible frequency to see if it resonates with your data.
